title: Indian Languages and Literature-II
summary: Old Apabhramsha took new forms. The alphabets of Ashoka's Brahmi were uneven; by Harsha's time the letters were regular. All scripts of present northern Indian languages except Urdu originated in old Brahmi (compare Gujarati, Hindi and Punjabi). Over 200 languages or dialects are spoken in India; twenty-two are in the Constitution (originally 15: Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kashmiri, Marathi, Oriya, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Sindhi, Urdu, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam; Nepali, Manipuri and Konkani were added later). Forms of Hindi: Braj Bhasha (Surdas, Bihari), Avadhi (Tulsidas), Bhojpuri, Magadhi, Maithili (Vidyapati), Rajasthani and Khadi Boli; Khusrau used Khadi Boli in the 13th century but its extensive literary use began in the 19th century.

Arabic and Persian came with the Turks and Mongols; Persian remained the court language for centuries. Urdu was born from the interaction of Turkish settlers and soldiers (after the conquest of Delhi in 1192) with the common people, a dialect that became a formal language in the Persian script, boosted in Bahmani states (Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bijapur, Berar), where it was called Dakshini. The earliest Urdu poet is Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), follower of Nizamuddin Auliya, with works such as Laila Majnun and Ayina-i-Sikandari; others: Ghalib, Zauq, Iqbal (Bang-i-Dara; 'Saare Jahan Se Achha'); prose: Ratan Nath Sarshar (Fasana-i-Azad), Premchand began in Urdu. The nazm is an Urdu form; Nawabs of Lucknow patronised it; the last Mughal Bahadur Shah Zafar wrote poetry; Pakistan has Urdu as state language. Persian literature: Babur's Tuzuk-i-Baburi (in Turkish, translated into Persian under Akbar), Humayun Nama, Akbar Nama and Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazl, Faizi, Badayuni, Chandra Bhan (Shah Jahan's days), Abdul Hamid Lahori's Badshah Nama, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, Tabaqat-i-Alamgiri; Noorjahan was a Persian poetess; Akbar had the Mahabharata, Gita and Upanishads translated into Persian; Minhaj-us-Siraj, Zia Barani and Ibn Battuta wrote in Persian; Amir Khusrau and Amir Hasan Dehlvi wrote Persian poetry.

Regional languages grew with the Bhakti movement and Sanskrit declined; Prithviraj Raso (about Prithviraj Chauhan) is considered the first Hindi book; Hindi evolved between the 7th–8th and 14th centuries (Veergatha Kala, Adi Kala, patronised by Rajputs). Devotional poetry followed: Tulsidas's Ramcharit Manas (Avadhi) based on Valmiki's Ramayana but deifies Rama (Valmiki's is a human hero) and adds folk scenes; Surdas's Sur Sagar (Braj) shows Krishna as an infant, a prankster and a young man with the gopis; Mirabai (Rajasthani), Raskhan, Nandadas, Rahim, Bhushan, Bihari (Satsai), Kabir (formless God). Rabindranath Tagore won the 1913 Nobel Prize for Geetanjali. Hindi prose came into its own in the 19th century: Bharatendu Harishchandra, Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi, Bankim Chandra's novels in translation (Vande Mataram is from Anandamath), Swami Dayanand (Satyartha Prakash; advocated Hindi as the common language), Premchand (Urdu to Hindi), Nirala, Mahadevi Verma (first woman writer to highlight women's issues), Maithili Sharan Gupt, Jaishankar Prasad, Ramchandra Shukla, Shyam Sundar Das, Pant, Dinkar, Bachchan. These writers wrote with a purpose.

Bengali: Baptist Mission Press at Serampore (1800), Fort William College (1800); Chaitanya's hymns and Mangal Kavyas; William Carey wrote a Bengali grammar and an English–Bengali dictionary; Macaulay's victory (1835), Wood's Despatch (1854), universities of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay (1857); Ram Mohan Roy, Vidyasagar, Akshay Kumar Dutta, Bankim Chandra, Sharat Chandra, R.C. Dutt, Rabindranath Tagore; nationalist poetry of Qazi Nazrul Islam (Bengali) and Subramania Bharati (Tamil). Assamese: buranjis, Shankardeva (Vaishnavism), Lakshminath Bezbaruah. Oriya: Saraladasa, Upendra Bhanja, Fakirmohan Senapati. Punjabi: Gurmukhi and Persian scripts; Guru Nanak first poet; Sufi Farid; Guru Tegh Bahadur and Guru Gobind Singh; love stories of Heer–Ranjha, Sassi–Punnu, Sohni–Mahiwal; Waris Shah's Heer; Bulleh Shah's kafis; Bhai Vir Singh (Rana Surat Singh). Rajasthani: bards; Colonel Todd's Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan; Mirabai. Gujarati: Narsi Mehta, Narmad, Govardhanram's Saraswatichandra, K.M. Munshi (Prithvi Vallabh). Sindhi: Sufis; Mirza Kalich Beg, Dewan Kauramal. Marathi: Jnaneshwar (13th century; kirtan tradition), Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram (greatest Bhakti poet), Ramdas (Shivaji's guru), Tilak's Kesari. Kashmiri: Kalhana's Rajatarangini (Sanskrit); Lal Ded (14th century, first to sing in Kashmiri), Habba Khatoon, Mahjoor, Nund Rishi, Dina Nath Nadim; literature lagged due to poverty, backwardness, lack of schools and Dogra preference for Dogri.

Europeans added new words to Indian languages. Missionaries published dictionaries and grammars, introduced lithographic presses for local-language literature and opened schools and colleges that taught local languages, producing an educated reading class. Indians wrote in English after 1835: Michael Madhusudan Dutt, Toru Dutt, Sarojini Naidu and Tagore (poetry); Surendranath Banerjea, Pherozeshah Mehta and Nehru (prose).

vsa: 'The Persian language was developed during the medieval period.' Support the statement with two points.

Persian was the court language for many centuries; Akbar had Sanskrit books and the Mahabharata translated into Persian; histories (Akbarnama, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, Badshahnama), poetry (Amir Khusrau, Faizi) and administrative manuals were written in it.
Mention the dialects used by Tulsidas and Surdas.
Tulsidas used Avadhi in the Ramcharitmanas and Surdas used Braj Bhasha in the Sur Sagar.
How did Dinanath Nadim contribute to Kashmiri literature?
He was among the poets who wrote devotional and modern poetry in Kashmiri, enriching its literature.
A Shaivite mystic of the 14th century, probably the first to sing in the Kashmiri language.
What was the role of the Christian missionaries in the growth of Indian languages?
They published the earliest dictionaries and grammars, introduced lithographic printing presses and established schools and colleges that taught local languages, producing an educated reading class.

Why is Waris Shah famous in Punjabi literature?

Name two Hindi poets of the Bhakti period and their works.
Tulsidas – Ramcharit Manas; Surdas – Sur Sagar; Bihari – Satsai; Mirabai – devotional songs (any two).
sa: Briefly describe the development of Hindi language.

Hindi evolved from Apabhramsha between the 7th–8th and the 14th century (Veergatha Kala), with Prithviraj Raso as the first book. Under the Bhakti movement it became devotional – Kabir, Tulsidas, Surdas, Mirabai. Khadi Boli, used by Khusrau, came into extensive literary use in the 19th century with Bharatendu Harishchandra, Dayanand, Premchand, Nirala and Mahadevi Verma.
What is the role of the Persian language in medieval India?

Persian was the court language, so histories, administrative manuals, letters (insha) and poetry were written in it; Mughal rulers patronised it and had Sanskrit works translated; Amir Khusrau, Faizi, Abul Fazl and Chandra Bhan wrote in it.
Write a note on Punjabi literature before the 19th century.

Guru Nanak was the first Punjabi poet; Sufi poets like Farid and later Bulleh Shah (kafis) and Waris Shah (Heer) wrote; Adi Granth contains poetry of the gurus; love stories of Heer–Ranjha, Sohni–Mahiwal and Sassi–Punnu gave themes; Gurmukhi was mostly confined to the Adi Granth.
Explain the role of Bhakti poets in the growth of regional languages.

Poets like Tulsidas, Surdas, Kabir, Mirabai, Jnaneshwar, Tukaram, Narsi Mehta and Shankardeva composed in the languages of the people, which spread them and made them literary languages as Sanskrit declined.
Describe the contribution of Rabindranath Tagore to Bengali literature.
Tagore (1861–1941) wrote novels, dramas, short stories, criticism, music and essays; he won the 1913 Nobel Prize for Geetanjali and influenced all India.
la: Examine the process of evolution of Northern Indian languages.

Old Apabhramsha took new forms; the Brahmi script of Ashoka became regular by Harsha's time and all northern scripts except Urdu came from it. Hindi grew in forms such as Braj, Avadhi, Maithili and Khadi Boli, with Prithviraj Raso as first book and the Bhakti poets giving devotional literature. Urdu arose after 1192 from Turks and locals and flourished in Deccan and Delhi; Persian was the court language. Punjabi, Bengali, Assamese, Oriya, Gujarati, Marathi, Sindhi and Kashmiri each developed with Bhakti and Sufi saints, missionaries' grammars and presses, and nationalism.
Describe the growth of Punjabi and its literature during medieval times.

Punjabi is written in Gurmukhi and Persian scripts. Guru Nanak was the first poet; Sufi saints like Farid used Punjabi, writing in the Persian script; the Adi Granth contains poetry of the gurus and Farid (15th–16th centuries); Guru Gobind Singh composed savaiyyas. Love stories (Heer–Ranjha, Sohni–Mahiwal, Sassi–Punnu) and the story of Puran Bhagat gave early themes; Waris Shah's Heer is a landmark; Bulleh Shah's kafis are sung with fervour.
Describe the development of Hindi literature from the Bhakti period to modern times.

Hindi literature began with heroic raso poetry (Prithviraj Raso) and became devotional under the Bhakti movement: Kabir (formless God), Tulsidas (Ramcharit Manas in Avadhi, deifying Rama), Surdas (Sur Sagar in Braj), Mirabai and Raskhan. In the 19th century prose grew with Bharatendu Harishchandra, Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi and Dayanand; later Premchand, Nirala, Jaishankar Prasad, Mahadevi Verma, Pant, Dinkar and Bachchan wrote with a purpose of social reform.
Explain the contribution of Christian missionaries and the press to Indian languages and literature.

Missionaries produced dictionaries and grammars (e.g. William Carey's Bengali grammar and dictionary), introduced lithographic presses that published local-language books and journals, and opened schools and colleges teaching local languages. This created an educated class that wanted to read, enriched vocabulary with new words and helped literature, newspapers and nationalism to grow.
